## Purpose

The purpose is to eliminate wasted memory from fixed sparse-cache sizes in hybrid linear attention by sizing the cache to actual per-step recall requirements.

Paper [1] (ZigZagkv) addresses non-uniform budget allocation across layers to reduce information loss — "allocate a uniform budget size for each layer to retain" is the problem they solve, which is closely related. Paper [9] (LoLA/hybrid sparse attention) directly addresses hybrid linear attention with sparse attention and token eviction, and discusses fixed-size recurrent states causing forgetfulness. Paper [24] (XKV) addresses "personalized KV cache memory reduction" with non-uniform allocation. Paper [1] specifically targets eliminating waste from fixed uniform budgets by adapting to actual layer needs — this is substantively equivalent to the purpose of eliminating waste from fixed cache sizes by adapting to actual recall requirements. The host architecture differs (standard transformer layers vs. hybrid linear attention), but the objective — replace fixed cache budget with adaptive sizing to avoid waste — is the same problem class.

## Mechanism

The mechanism is SRE-adaptive-mass caching: a training-free method that retains tokens until a target fraction p of total Self-Recall Error (SRE) mass is captured, dynamically adjusting cache size at each update step.

The SRE metric itself (measuring how well the linear attention recurrent state can recall past tokens) appears to be specific to paper [9]'s framework. However, the broader primitive of "retain tokens until a target fraction of some importance/attention mass is captured" appears in several papers. Paper [13] (FlexPrefill) uses "cumulative attention score threshold" to dynamically determine how many tokens to attend to — retaining tokens until a target fraction of attention mass is captured. Paper [30] (RCStat) uses RC-based thresholding for KV compression. Paper [14] (STR) uses probabilistic selection that dynamically adjusts token retention. The specific primitive of "accumulate a mass metric until a threshold fraction p is reached" as the cache-sizing rule is most directly matched by [13]'s cumulative attention threshold approach — same underlying primitive of threshold-on-cumulative-mass, different metric name.

## Evaluation

The evaluation uses RULER long-context benchmarks against LoLA's fixed cache size baseline.

RULER is a named benchmark family used for long-context LLM evaluation. Paper [9] (LoLA) itself uses RULER. Paper [16] (SCBench) evaluates long-context methods. Multiple papers in this set evaluate on long-context benchmarks. The evaluation design — running on RULER benchmark with comparison to a baseline — is a standard evaluation design used in prior work (paper [9] explicitly).
